summary: A brief transitional passage, then the Gemara continues: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a non-priest who sets up the wood arrangement on the altar (sidur etzim) is liable for the death penalty. Rabbi Zeira objects: is there any Temple service valid when performed by a non-priest but also a death-penalty offense? The discussion refines Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and establishes the precise conditions under which wood-arrangement is considered a complete service requiring priestly status.

glossary.en: Liable to death penalty; a non-priest who performs certain Temple services is liable to death at the hand of Heaven.
Complete service; a Temple task that is a full, standalone act of divine service requiring priesthood.

display.title: A one-line bridge: from the resolved young-bull difficulty to R. Yochanan's new ruling
display.hint: Connects the previous analysis to R. Yochanan's new ruling.

learning.learnerQuestion: What is this single transitional line doing between the resolved young-bull difficulty on the previous page and R. Yochanan's new ruling about non-priests and wood arrangement?
learning.coreTension: The Gemara could move straight from Rav Hamnuna's now-resolved difficulty into R. Yochanan's new statement, but instead inserts a brief connector first.
learning.coreMove: This line closes the verse-by-verse derivation from 27a so that R. Yochanan's ruling on non-priest wood arrangement, cited in R. Asi's name, opens cleanly as its own topic.

takeaway.text: Not every line in the Gemara carries independent content - some exist purely to mark a clean break between one finished discussion and the next, and a learner should not search this line for substantive teaching it does not contain.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara signals a new topic is beginning by first finishing the old one, even in a single line.
learning.learningBlocker: There is no substantive content to extract from this line beyond its structural role - it should not be read as adding anything to either the preceding verse-derivation or the coming ruling.
learning.memoryAnchor: A paragraph break: closing the previous page's analysis before opening R. Yochanan's new ruling.

argumentFlow.label: Transition
argumentFlow.text: Brief passage connecting the Rav Hamnuna difficulty to R. Yochanan's new ruling.

misconceptions.misconception: This is a major independent passage with its own teaching.
misconceptions.correction: It is only a transitional connector closing the previous discussion before R. Yochanan's new ruling begins.

quizSeeds.question: What is the brief passage at the start of 27b?
quizSeeds.answer: A transitional connector from the previous discussion about non-priest services to R. Yochanan's new ruling.

display.title: Valid but punishable: R. Zeira's paradox and R. Yochanan's revised wood-arrangement ruling
display.whats: R. Yochanan rules that a non-priest who sets up the wood arrangement on the altar incurs the death penalty. R. Zeira objects: every service incurring the death penalty must also be invalid when done by a non-priest. R. Yochanan's ruling is revised multiple times to account for these objections.
display.hint: The criterion is whether wood-arrangement is a 'complete service' (avodah temimah). If it is, a non-priest doing it both transgresses and renders the service invalid.

learning.learnerQuestion: If a non-priest who arranges the wood on the altar is liable to death, how can the wood arrangement also remain valid - aren't 'liable to death' and 'service stays valid' supposed to be mutually exclusive?
learning.coreTension: R. Zeira objects that R. Yochanan's ruling seems to describe an impossible combination: every other Temple service that incurs the death penalty for a non-priest also disqualifies the offering when he performs it, yet R. Yochanan says the non-priest is liable to death for wood arrangement without saying the arrangement itself is invalid.
learning.coreMove: Through several rounds of objection and revision, the Gemara narrows R. Yochanan's ruling: it first confirms that a non-priest can transgress and be punished while the wood arrangement itself remains valid, so the two categories are not actually mutually exclusive; further objections then require that the service be both a daytime service and a 'complete service' (avodah temimah) before the death penalty applies. Mar Zutra closes the daf by asking exactly what the now several-times-revised ruling actually covers.

takeaway.text: A ruling that initially looks like a flat contradiction - valid yet punishable - survives because transgressing a prohibition and invalidating an offering are not the same axis; whether the two align depends on whether the act counts as a 'complete service.'

learning.ahaMoment: Liable to death and the offering remaining valid are not mutually exclusive after all - a non-priest can transgress a prohibition and be punished for it without that transgression by itself disqualifying the service, as long as the act is not classified as a full, independent 'complete service.'
learning.learningBlocker: Mar Zutra's question, exactly what R. Yochanan's now several-times-revised ruling covers, is left open at the end of 27b; the daf does not pin down whether the death penalty applies to wood arrangement broadly or to some narrower piece of it - that precision is only supplied on the following daf, where Rava identifies the two-log placement specifically as the 'complete service' in question.
learning.memoryAnchor: Death penalty without invalidation: a non-priest can be punished for touching the altar fire without his act voiding the offering - unless that act counts as a full, independent service.

argumentFlow.label: R. Yochanan: non-priest wood arranger = death
argumentFlow.text: R. Asi citing R. Yochanan: a non-priest who sets up the wood arrangement on the altar is liable to death.

argumentFlow.label: R. Zeira: valid non-priest service cannot also be punishable
argumentFlow.text: R. Zeira: is there any service that is valid when performed by a non-priest but also punishable? These categories seem contradictory.

argumentFlow.label: Is there no such case?
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara wonders: is there truly no Temple service that is valid by a non-priest but still punishable?

argumentFlow.label: Revised ruling: non-priest transgresses but service valid
argumentFlow.text: Revision of R. Yochanan's position: the wood arrangement is valid even if done by a non-priest (the service is not disqualified), but the non-priest has transgressed.

argumentFlow.label: Further difficulty: daytime + complete service
argumentFlow.text: Additional objections: the ruling must specify that this is a daytime service AND a complete service before the death penalty applies.

argumentFlow.label: Mar Zutra's query
argumentFlow.text: Mar Zutra asks what exactly R. Yochanan's ruling covers, given all the objections and revisions.

halachic: death penalty for non-priest Temple service
theological: Temple service as exclusively priestly domain
narrative: multiple rounds of revision to R. Yochanan's ruling

requiresUnderstanding: death penalty for priestly service violation

misconceptions.misconception: Any service a non-priest performs validly, he may also do without penalty.
misconceptions.correction: R. Zeira shows this assumption breaks down for wood arrangement: a non-priest can be punished for the act even though the service itself remains valid.

misconceptions.misconception: Wood arrangement performed by a non-priest automatically invalidates the altar service.
misconceptions.correction: R. Yochanan's revised ruling holds that the arrangement may still be valid even though the non-priest has transgressed and is liable to death.

visualizableElements.label: Valid vs punishable service categories
visualizableElements.description: Three categories: (1) complete priestly service - non-priest is punished AND service is invalid; (2) non-priestly service - non-priest may do it validly; (3) the problematic middle category

visualizableElements.label: Non-priest at the altar fire
visualizableElements.description: A non-kohen placing logs on the altar fire - does this transgress and/or invalidate the service?

quizSeeds.question: What paradox does R. Zeira identify in R. Yochanan's ruling about non-priests arranging wood?
quizSeeds.answer: If a service is valid when performed by a non-priest, it should not be punishable; if it is punishable, the service should be invalid. 'Valid but punishable' seems contradictory.

quizSeeds.question: What is the revised understanding of R. Yochanan's ruling about wood arrangement?
quizSeeds.answer: The wood arrangement remains valid even if performed by a non-priest, but the non-priest has transgressed a prohibition - he is punishable but the service is not disqualified.

sugyot.finalRuling: Non-priest wood arrangement: the ruling and its precise conditions are debated and revised across 27b-28a. The service may be valid while the non-priest transgresses.
